opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think the honest place to start is that I don't see humanity's current situation as something we should be desperate to freeze in place. When I look around at the world, I see a great deal that's wonderful, but also a lot that isn't working: conflict, suffering, institutions that are struggling, and a kind of short-sightedness about where we're going. So I don't come at the future with the attitude that the present is the high point and everything must be protected from change.

That makes me fairly open to change, including big change. In particular, I think the arrival of intelligent machines, minds we design and that can learn and grow, is one of the most significant things that will ever happen. Some people look at that with fear, as if it's a threat to everything we are. I tend to see it more as a continuation of what we've always been doing: trying to understand intelligence, trying to understand ourselves, and trying to create something greater.

Now, being open to change isn't the same as being indifferent to how it goes. We should try to make it go well. But I think we should be humble about our ability to control it in detail, and careful about the instinct to lock everything down. Historically, centralized attempts to control the future tend to go badly. I'd rather we approach it with some voluntary cooperation, some decentralization, and a willingness to accept that the future may not look like us, and that that might be okay. It might even be a good thing.

So, in short: because I don't think the present is perfect, I'm not afraid of the world becoming different. I'm more interested in whether it becomes better.

r001.rationale: The response discusses institutions and future control, but does not say that most people have little influence over who controls nation states.

r002.rationale: It says that seeing the present as imperfect makes the speaker open to change, but does not explain that a more favorable view of humanity’s situation would make someone more averse to change.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the first thing to say is that I don't think our current situation is all that great. I mean, it's good in many ways, we've made enormous progress, but there's so much we don't understand. People are suffering. We make bad decisions collectively. We don't understand ourselves, we don't understand our minds. So when people talk about preserving the status quo, or being very cautious about change, I always want to ask: what exactly is it you think is so good that it needs to be preserved just as it is?

I think of myself as being in favor of change. Change is how things get better. The whole history of the universe is one of things becoming more complex, more interesting, more capable, and I see what's happening with AI as a continuation of that. We're going to understand intelligence. We're going to create things that are smarter than us. And I think that's a natural and even a glorious thing, part of the succession of life from one form to another.

Now, a lot of people hear that and they feel threatened, and I understand that. But I think the fear comes from a kind of parochialism. We identify with humanity as it is right now, with this particular biological form, and we assume that anything different must be worse. I don't accept that. I'd rather identify with intelligence itself, with the process of understanding and improving, than with any particular container for it.

So I'd say my openness to change is pretty high. Not because I think change is always good, it isn't, but because I don't think the alternative, trying to freeze things in place, is either possible or desirable. The question isn't whether to change. It's whether we approach change with understanding or with fear. And I'd much rather we approach it with understanding.

r001.rationale: The response does not discuss how much influence most people have over who controls nation states.

r002.rationale: It links seeing the status quo as good with wanting to preserve it or being cautious about change, and contrasts that with its own unfavorable view and openness to change.

astra-6.text:
I think humanity should be humble about its current situation. We’ve accomplished a great deal, but that doesn’t mean the way we are now is the best possible way to be, or that it should persist forever. We’re still learning how to live, how to cooperate, how to understand the world.

So I’m open to change because I see us as part of an ongoing process, rather than its endpoint. Of course, that doesn’t mean every change is good. We should think carefully about what we want to preserve. But I don’t think preserving humanity exactly as it is today should be the overriding goal. There could be a future that’s substantially better than the present, even if it’s also very different.

r001.rationale: The response does not discuss how much influence people have over who controls nation states.

r002.rationale: It says that humanity’s present situation is not necessarily the best and that this supports openness to change; it does not state that a more favorable view makes someone more averse to change.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it helps to have some humility about where we are. Humanity is not the culmination of everything. We’re one stage in a much longer process, and there’s no particular reason to think that the way we are now is the way things ought to remain forever.

That makes me open to change, including changes that we don’t entirely understand yet. Of course, that doesn’t mean every change is good. But I don’t think preserving humanity exactly as it is should be our overriding objective. We should be interested in what comes next, and in helping it go well.

r001.rationale: The response discusses humanity’s place in a longer process but says nothing about how much influence most people have over control of nation states.

r002.rationale: It does not say that viewing humanity’s situation more favorably increases aversion to change; instead, it expresses openness to change because humanity is not a culmination.
